title: Low and stable inflation
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:37Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new
2026-11-01T14:55:59Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

match.reason: The new point combines the RBA's 2 to 3 per cent average target with underlying (core) inflation, but no single bank point covers both: eco-inflation-target has the target without underlying inflation, and eco-headline-underlying-inflation has underlying inflation without the target, so a new point is safer than a wrong match.

draft.title: Low and stable inflation
card: Low and stable inflation is one of Australia's three economic goals. The Reserve Bank aims for inflation of 2 to 3 per cent a year, on average over time.
Inflation is measured by the consumer price index (CPI). It tracks the change in the price of a fixed basket of goods and services that households buy.
Some prices jump around, such as fruit and vegetables after a flood, or fuel after a global price shock. These can push the CPI up or down for a short time.
Underlying (core) inflation leaves out these prices that jump around. It gives a clearer view of the lasting trend in inflation.
draft.remember: The goal is 2 to 3 per cent on average. Underlying inflation shows the trend behind the CPI.

a.q: Why do economists look at underlying inflation as well as the CPI?
opts: It removes short-term price jumps to show the trend
It includes only the prices of essential goods
It measures price changes for businesses, not households
It shows how much wages have risen over the year
a.why: Underlying inflation strips out prices that jump around, so it shows the lasting trend. It is not limited to essentials, because it still covers most of the basket. The CPI already measures prices paid by households.
a.clue: Think about what a sudden flood does to vegetable prices.

b.q: After a drought, fruit prices in Australia jump and lift the CPI for one quarter. Other prices rise slowly. What does underlying inflation most likely show?
opts: A lower rate than the CPI, as fruit prices are left out
A higher rate than the CPI, as fruit prices are left out
The same rate as the CPI, as it counts every price
A rate of zero, as it ignores all price changes
b.why: Underlying inflation leaves out prices that jump around, so the fruit spike does not lift it. It is likely lower than the CPI for that quarter. It is not the same as the CPI, because the two use different sets of prices.
b.clue: Which measure still contains the fruit price jump?

a.best: It removes short-term price jumps to show the trend

b.best: A lower rate than the CPI, as fruit prices are left out

check.summary: No problems found. The card accurately covers the RBA's 2 to 3 per cent target, the CPI and underlying inflation at a level suited to VCE, and both questions have one clearly correct answer that matches the explanations.
